articleTitle: Discrimination and nuisance tripping of residual current-operated devices in domestic and similar installations
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: Considerable progress has been achieved during the last few years in protection against electric shock. IEC-Standard 364 mentions two barriers against electric shock that is protection against electric shock in normal service (basic protection, protection against direct contact) and protection against electric shock in case of fault (fault protection, protection against indirect contact). The author examines fault discrimination and nuisance tripping of residual current protective devices for use in domestic and similar applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Selecting standby generating plants for buildings
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The selection of standby generators for buildings used to be a simple matter of assessing the total power demand of essential equipment in a building and then procuring the most economical set which satisfies the minimum technical requirement. The author assesses the problem of selecting the correct standby generator, bearing in mind technical and environmental requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical installation in a 3 km long cable tunnel in Hong Kong
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The 275 kV cable connection between Lamma power station and Kennedy Road substation in Hong Kong island included a 3150 m section inside a underground cable tunnel, which was designed to cater for two circuits of 275 kV oil-filled cable at present, but with space and provision to add six circuits of 132 kV XLPE cable and four circuits of 11 kV XLPE cable in future. Forced air ventilation was provided for cooling the two circuits of 275 kV cable at present. For increased heat dissipation in the future, closed circuit chilled water cooling systems will be provided. Ventilation plants and auxiliary power supply substations of the cable tunnel are located in the Wah Fu portal (south end) and the Bowen portal (north end). All services were designed for unmanned operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Co-ordination and discrimination in low voltage installations-simple with HRC fuses
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The IEE Wiring Regulations specify the requirements necessary for safe installation and recent Health and Safety legislation has made factory owners and installation designers more aware of their responsibilities. The June 1987 amendments of the Regulations has focussed attention on the question of discrimination and co-ordination in electrical installations. With the significant improvements achieved in the standardisation of HRC fuses, and the emergence of compact and competitive fusegear, the author reviews the role of the HRC fuse in existing and future low voltage electrical installations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: To the electrical installation designer, installer and commissioning engineer, it is the integration of services which creates the intelligence in a building and its electrical installation. The author investigates quality in intelligent installations by examining large and small, commercial and industrial, applications of intelligent buildings.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of the personal micro for the design and analysis of an electrical power circuit
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: While it is accepted that there are a number of computer programs available which claim to design low voltage electrical circuits to comply with the 15th Edition of the IEE Wiring Regulations, in using one, an engineer is relying upon the integrity and accuracy of its compiler. He is also limited to the ground covered by the program and its particular approach. Today we are in a situation where many professional electrical engineers have their own microcomputer with disc drives for fast retrieval of data and means of printing and/or displaying the output. This has become the logical follow-on from logarithms, slide rules and calculators. By virtue of their education and training, these engineers are capable of making use of this very versatile tool and the authors attempt to indicate how it can be used to their advantage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The designers of lighting layout schemes for commercial offices operating under a number of constraints which limit their freedom of action and which, inadvertently, lead to the inefficient and wasteful use of electricity. Traditional installation and control methods severely restrict the freedom of the electrical engineer to modify such layouts to meet the changing needs of the client and/or achieve a reduction in general lighting running costs. The authors describe how the internal telephone network can be used to obtain totally flexible control over the local lighting environment. An installation is described where use of the system has eliminated the need for general switchwiring, the running cost of the lighting has been dramatically reduced and the client has total flexibility to alter switching patterns to meet constantly changing occupant requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: Large installations are increasingly benefiting from UPS systems today, but the real needs for such systems should be objectively assessed before a UPS is specified. If and when the benefits have been clearly established, it becomes more straightforward to establish the optimum system components from the bewildering range of battery types and sizes, chargers, inverters, changeover switches, instrumentation, controls and environmental impact characteristics. Only then does specifying, installing and maintaining a UPS system become routine. The author reviews all these aspects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cable management systems for raised floors
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: Over the past two or three years the wide spread use of raised floors has dominated the way in which buildings are cabled. In the UK the use of raised floors as a means of providing cable management has been adopted much more readily than in other countries. Accepting the fact that raised floors have now become an essential building component, the author examines the current trends in cable management technology to work within these floors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Inspection and testing of electrical installations
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The author indicates the purpose and intent of the initial and periodic inspection and testing required by the IEE Regulations for Electrical Installations (15th Edition)-the 'Wiring Regulations'. The author does not intend primarily to describe in detail the testing methods but rather to consider the logic, philosophy and purpose of the tests and the order in which they are done. The different considerations relating to the initial and the periodic inspection and testing are discussed and the differing relative emphasis on inspection and on testing in the two cases are considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Solid state solutions to some protection grading problems
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The author sets out to show how the problems faced by protection grading engineers, which have become more intense in recent years, may be reduced by the use of solid-state protective relays in preference to electro-mechanical relays. The author has no particular manufacturer in mind (most of the major relay manufacturers produce suitable solid-state relays) but for the sake of simplicity concentrates on the GEC MCGG relay.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Installation and maintenance benefits of plug-in control modules for lighting energy management
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The keys to viable energy management schemes are high energy saving, coupled with low installation costs, thereby giving short financial payback periods. In lighting, high energy savings are achieved only with flexible control systems which ensure that only those lights really needed are switched on, and that all others are automatically switched off. Ideally lights should be controlled on a person by person basis or, failing this, then at least on a work area basis. Field trials have shown that personnel will also turn lights off when not needed providing that it is easy to do so without leaving the work place. The ability to override the system locally is an important psychological factor in ensuring acceptance of an energy management system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: Energy problems and cost in the last ten years have stimulated new lighting techniques, which can save energy and improve lighting standards. Four factors are prominent in controlling the energy consumed by electric lighting: (1) the amount of light given; (2) the measures adopted to control and distribute the light; (3) the choice of light source and circuit; (4) the techniques used to manage the lights. The author examines items (3) and (4). The standards for interior lighting, in quantity and quality, are defined in the CIBSE code for interior lighting, which shows that satisfactory performance is determined by illuminance, uniformity, brightness balance, discomfort glare, veiling reflections and colour parameters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Some aspects of precautions against electric shock and earth faults in electrical installations
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The author reviews some of the many and varied requirements relating to protection against earth faults, earth leakage and electric shock in the design of 50 Hz, 415 volts, 3 phase and 240 volts, single phase electrical installations together with the application of relevant protective devices. In particular, it distinguishes between the application of residual current devices to provide what is commonly called 'personnel protection', protection against fires and protection to comply with requirements of the IEE Wiring Regulations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Successful selection and operation of overcurrent and residual current protective measures
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: Most basic electrical protective measures are intended to ensure that significant electrical energy cannot be dissipated anywhere other than within current using equipment. These measures include primary and secondary insulation, enclosures, barriers etc., and they have a passive function. Active measures are generally arranged to interrupt the supply to a circuit when electrical energy dissipation becomes excessive either within the circuit conductors and current using equipment or outside the circuit (for example in a person) where no dissipation is intended. The author examines active protective measures generally and describes the conditions necessary to ensure their successful operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An alternative approach to the design of standby power systems
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The authors review three of the commonly available types of AC UPS; static, rotary and diesel rotary. The relative merits of their electrical performance are discussed. In particular it is considered how their operational characteristics reflect upon the overall design and performance of the standby power system. The conclusion drawn from this comparative exercise is that optimising the design of a standby system is conditional upon the acceptability of a complete 'systems' approach being adopted. The authors also highlight an alternative approach to the design of standby power system which offers certain merits.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Installation practice within the pharmaceutical industry
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The authors detail current electrical engineering installation practice within the pharmaceutical industry and is generally related to one particular project, namely a new pharmaceutical research and development building now nearing completion for Glaxo Group Research Ltd. at Ware, Hertfordshire, England. This building is at present the largest R&D project within Europe. Various topics are covered and these include the HV/LV network, general power and lighting installations, data and communications, and other ancillary services. The authors expand and detail one or two items of interest that evolved during the design and construction period. These include modifications made to the distribution network, comparative cost studies of alternative lighting schemes, methods of achieving good building management system control, project management etc.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Electrical installations for vehicular traffic tunnels
publicationTitle: Third International Conference on Installation Engineering Designing and Maintaining Successful Systems, 1988.
abstract: The safe passage of traffic through road tunnels requires 24-hour per day availability of the many electrically based systems provided in these tunnels. These systems have to operate under hostile environmental conditions, with limited opportunities for maintenance because of the paramount need to keep traffic flowing. For capital cost reasons they have to be designed and installed without, if possible, increasing the minimum geometric dimensions of the tunnel established to allow passage of the designed traffic. The author argues that safe passage of traffic may be said to be attained if the systems provided ensure that the flow of traffic can pass through the tunnel with about the same speed, degree of safety and comfort as is present along the adjacent stretches of road. Traffic flow can be safe and smooth only when sufficient visual information is available concerning the 'run of the road' and the presence (or absence) of obstacles, including vehicles and their movements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
